title: GPPT: Graph Pre-training and Prompt Tuning to Generalize Graph Neural Networks

problem.claim: Supervised graph neural network training requires large amounts of labeled data for each application.

gap.claim: Existing graph pre-training methods leave an inherent training-objective gap between pretext and downstream tasks, making adaptation costly and potentially harming downstream performance.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes graph pre-training and prompt tuning (GPPT) as a transfer learning paradigm for generalizing graph neural networks.
GPPT pre-trains GNNs with masked edge prediction and uses a graph prompting function to convert a node classification instance into a token-pair edge-prediction formulation.
The reformulation enables pre-trained GNNs to perform node classification through token-pair linking probabilities without tedious fine-tuning.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe GPPT as a novel transfer learning paradigm.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on eight benchmark datasets report an average improvement of 4.29% in few-shot graph analysis.
The authors report that GPPT accelerates model convergence by up to 4.32X.
The authors report that implementation code is available on GitHub.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNN supervision requires substantial labeled data for each application.
Graph transfer learning pre-trains GNNs and fine-tunes them with few downstream labels.
Pretext and downstream objectives differ, causing costly adaptation and possible downstream deterioration.
GPPT uses masked edge pre-training and graph prompting to represent node classification as edge prediction over candidate-label and node token pairs.
Experiments on eight benchmark datasets report improved few-shot performance and faster convergence.

source_observation.claim: A mismatch between pre-training and downstream objectives can make transfer adaptation costly.

interpretation.claim: Transfer methods may benefit from reformulating downstream tasks to resemble the pre-training objective.

application.claim: When designing few-shot transfer systems, consider task or input transformations that preserve compatibility with the pre-trained prediction task.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that this strategy is effective beyond the reported graph node-classification setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the eight benchmark datasets, baselines, experimental settings, or statistical variability.
The abstract does not describe the pre-training data, model architecture, or detailed prompting procedure.
